entries.title: Afghanistan five years of Taliban rule: Has Germany kept its promises?
entries.summary: After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring all the Afghan local staff members to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
entries.content:
Germany

Afghanistan, the Taliban and German promises

August 11, 2026

After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring all the Afghan local staff members to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June this year, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2500 ($2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Courtruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was cancelled."

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses
entries.summary: The explosion of a Ukrainian decoy drone in Bulgaria near the Romanian border reveals gaps in Bulgaria's defenses, raises questions and shines a light on the country's policy shift on the war in Ukraine.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses

August 11, 2026

The explosion of a Ukrainian decoy drone in Bulgaria near the Romanian border reveals gaps in Bulgaria's defenses, raises questions and shines a light on the country's policy shift on the war in Ukraine.

When a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from.

Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems.

And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged.

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable."

Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident.

What is known about the incident?

At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania.

Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field.

In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives."

Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged.

Drone came down near gas pipeline

The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine, and in close proximity to a Romanian station.

This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target.

Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low.

Wake-up call for Bulgaria

Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability.

"Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT.

While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania, these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach.

Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though he admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country.

"Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one.

With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Was Russia involved?

As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria.

According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated.

Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals.

He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective.

The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication.

Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response

Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash.

"The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case.

As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine.

The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine.

Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador.

"This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position.

A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party.

While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy, promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine.

Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine, blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine.

"I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows
entries.summary: The summer heat is not only causing water levels in Germany's key river arteries to drop to dangerously low levels, but also contributing to wildfires in several areas. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows

Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026

The summer heat is not only causing water levels in Germany's key river arteries to drop to dangerously low levels, but also contributing to wildfires in several areas. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Economic experts expect cuts to industrial production because of reduced cargo shipping on the Rhine river
  • All shipping past the town of Kaub has now stopped due to record low levels
  • Wildfires caused the temporary closure of a major autobahn in northern Germany
  • The number of children involved in road accidents has increased

Join us as we cover these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany on Tuesday, August 8.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Some shipping stops on Rhine as level keeps dropping

Some shipping stops on Rhine as level keeps dropping

New record-low water levels have been measured on the Rhine, a vital transport waterway, with some cargo vessel owners stopping shipping on river sections in the south.

The inland navigation agency WSV reported that the gauge at Kaub, near Koblenz, had fallen to an all-time low of 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) on Tuesday, indicating that the river depth is about 115 centimeters at its deepest point .

A commodity trader told the Reuters news agency that it was "no longer to book cargo shipments on the Rhine past Kaub."

"Most sailings there have stopped," the trader said.

Traders said that sailings on ⁠northern ​sections of the river were continuing.

Germany, along with much of Europe, has experienced a series of heat waves and a long period without meaningful rainfall this summer, leading to low water levels in several rivers.

The situation is having not only an environmental but also an economic impact, with companies that are reliant on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls.

The ships that are still sailing are carrying much lighter loads than usual and at higher prices.

Skip next section In pictures: Rhine water levels hit historic low

In pictures: Rhine water levels hit historic low

Skip next section Endurance athlete to swim 200 kilometers from Frankfurt to Cologne for child water safety

Endurance athlete to swim 200 kilometers from Frankfurt to Cologne for child water safety

The 31-year-old endurance swimmer Nathalie Pohl took to the water in the Main River in Frankfurt on Tuesday at the start of a planned 200-kilometer (125-mile) swim to Cologne.

Pohl intends to swim via the Main and Rhine rivers to her destination over four days in a feat aimed at drawing attention to the importance of safe swimming, particularly for children.

According to figures from the German Livesaving Association (DLRG), at least 261 people have died by drowning this year up to the end of July.

The action is intended to raise money for swimming projects and education.

Swim not without risks

She is being accompanied by other swimmers who will put in one-hour sessions between her two-hour stints in the water.

Ahead of the start, Pohl showed herself unfazed by the possibility that low water levels in the Rhine could mean a weaker current at her and her team's back.

"Enough water is there and it shouldn't be a problem," she told the German DPA news agency, saying, however, that she hoped the algae that thrive in low water would not affect her health.

Pohl received a special permit for her action, with German authorities fundamentally warning against swimming in large rivers.

"Ultimately, something can always happen," she said, while stressing that she and her team had a comprehensive safety concept.

Skip next section What you need to know about low river water levels

What you need to know about low river water levels

Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by about 80%.

The water shortage comes during a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change.

But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels?

The Rhine: A vital transport waterway

The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times.

It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal.

As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively.

What are river gauge measurements?

The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course.

These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline.

This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more.

For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm.

Why is the gauge at Kaub so important?

Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim.

This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places.

It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine.

The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018.

The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days.

Skip next section Child road accidents rising steadily

Child road accidents rising steadily

More children were killed or injured in road accidents in 2025 than in in the previous year. That represents a renewed rise in road deaths and injuries affecting children since a decline during the coronavirus pandemic, statistics show.

Altogether 29,270 children under the age of 15 were injured in traffic accidents in Germany last year, a 7% increase over 2024, the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Monday.

The number of children killed in such accidents also rose from 53 in 2024 to 74 in 2025.

Of those fatalities, 30 were children under 6, well up on the number of children in that age group that were killed in 2024 (18).

The largest increase in deaths was seen in children travelling in cars (21 to 31).

The number of children killed on their bicycles in 2025 rose to 13 from 8 the previous year, while 4 were killed riding e-scooters, compared with none in 2024.

Most of the children involved in road traffic accidents in 2025 were riding a bicycle (34%). Altogether 31% were in a car, 20% were on foot and 8% were travelling on an e-scooter when the accidents occurred

"On average, a child was injured or killed in a road traffic accident every 18 minutes in 2025," Destatis said.

Skip next section Germany needs planned intelligence agency reforms, top politician says

Germany needs planned intelligence agency reforms, top politician says

The chairman of the parliamentary panel overseeing Germany's secret services, Marc Henrichmann, has defended the new powers planned for intelligence agencies.

"The latest security incident at the Leipzig freight airport has shown once again that we are dealing with a new quality of hybrid threats," Henrichmann told the daily Rheinische Post.

An explosives-laden unmanned aerial vehicle was flown into the airport last week.

Henrichmannsaid that cyber attacks, sabotage and unauthorized drone overflights were "now part of a reality for which we have to be better prepared."

For this reason, he said, both the foreign intelligence agency (BND) and the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) needed the "necessary legal and technical options" to detect threats early on and identify their sources.

The reform plans have met with criticism from civil liberty activists.

The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) has voiced fears that they could lead to a "massive increase in power for intelligence agencies.

"The BND and BfV are to be allowed to intervene profoundly in basic rights with expanded use of government spyware, AI analyses practically without protective measures, access to private video cameras and even hack-backs although the legal hurdles often remain vague and too low," the organization's Kai Dittmann said.

He called for the draft bill to be thoroughly revised, calling it "unconstitutional in many parts."

The draft reform bill is set to be approved by the German Cabinet on Wednesday.

Skip next section Autobahn reopens after closure because of wildfire

Autobahn reopens after closure because of wildfire

A highway in the northern state of Lower Saxony has reopened after being closed for over 12 hours as wildfire smoke dangerously reduced visibility.

Police closed the A7 autobahn to traffic between Göttingen and Kassel on Monday afternoon after thick smoke from the fire near Hannoversch Münden engulfed the road.

A police spokeswoman said some clean-up operations on a section of the motorway went on until the early hours of Tuesday morning but that both sides could now be used.

Skip next section Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute

Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute

The reduction in cargo being shipped via the Rhine because of low water levels will lead companies to cut production, a leading economic research institute reports.

"Transport routes south of Kaub are now threatening to become completely severed, meaning the Rhine is cut in two," Thomas Puls, the transport expert from the German Economic Institute (IW) told the daily Rheinische Post.

"Because neither road nor rail are able to take the goods needed, the most likely reaction of primary industries will be to reduce production," he said.

This assessment appeared to be confirmed by a spokesman for the chemical company Covestro, who told the paper that the shortfalls in supply caused by the disruption to Rhine shipping was already affecting production.

The spokesman said that the current lifting of a ban on trucks using the motorway on Sundays would be of only temporary benefit.

"Ship transport via the Rhine can barely be compensated on the road, as a cargo vessel that can carry 1,500 tons is the equivalent of around 60 trucks," he said. "So ship transport cannot be completely shifted to roads."

The record low water levels on the Rhine caused by a prolonged shortage of rainfall in Germany mean that ships are currently able to carry only around a fifth of the load they usually transport.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A warm guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

And, as has so often been the case recently, that very river is at the focus of our reporting from Germany as low water levels cause major disruption to cargo shipping and thus potentially to the industries that depend on it.

Another main topic is the threat to national security from hybrid forms of warfare, as reflected in recent drone incidents at sensitive sites. 

The government is moving to give intelligence agencies new powers to combat this threat, something that some see as a danger to civil liberties.

And we also take a look at statistics showing that road accidents involving children are on the rise again after a reduction during the coronavirus pandemic.

entries.title: Vietnam's VinSpace taps SpaceX for first satellite launches
entries.summary: Vietnam's first private space company is turning to Elon Musk's SpaceX to get its first satellites into orbit. The deal comes as Vietnam steps up efforts to build its own space industry and become a regional space power.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

Vietnam's first private space company is turning to Elon Musk's SpaceX to get its first satellites into orbit. The deal comes as Vietnam steps up efforts to build its own space industry and become a regional space power.

Vietnam's only private space company on Tuesday signed a deal with SpaceX to launch its first satellites into orbit next year.

The satellites will fly aboard a 2027 mission under SpaceX's Transporter rideshare program, which allows multiple customers to share the same rocket and split satellite launch costs.

What do we know about VinSpace and SpaceX?

The company, VinSpace, said it would develop and operate the satellites itself, using the missions to test technology in orbit and pave the way for future commercial services.

"Reliable access to space is fundamental to turning satellite innovation into operational missions," VinSpace CEO Thu Vu said.

The company did not disclose how many satellites it plans to launch, their specifications or the value of the contract with Elon Musk's SpaceX.

What is VinSpace?

VinSpace was established in November 2025 by Vingroup, Vietnam's largest privately-owned conglomerate.

The group was founded by Pham Nhat Vuong, Vietnam's richest man. It has interests ranging from real estate, retail and tourism to healthcare and education.

In recent years, Vingroup has increasingly expanded into technology, including electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, robotics and aerospace.

VinSpace says it ultimately wants to become a full-service aerospace company, with capabilities spanning satellite design and manufacturing, launch management, satellite operations and space-based data services.

What are Vietnam's ambitions in space?

Vietnam has been building its space capabilities for decades but remains a relatively small player in the global industry.

It launched its first telecommunications satellite in 2008 and a second in 2012.

The government has set a goal of becoming a mid-level space power in Southeast Asia by 2030, with satellite technology seen as part of a wider drive to develop high-tech industries.

In March, Vietnam opened a major space science and technology center at Hanoi's Hoa Lac High-Tech Park, aimed at expanding domestic satellite development and the use of space-based data.

In April, Vietnam licensed SpaceX's Starlink for its first large-scale trial of satellite internet, which uses thousands of low-Earth-orbit satellites to provide high-speed connectivity.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Syria sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia
entries.summary: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. The ruling comes over a year and a half after the dictator was overthrown and fled to Russia.
entries.content:
Syria

Syria sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia

August 11, 2026

A Syrian court has sentenced ousted President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. The ruling comes over a year and a half after the dictator was overthrown and fled to Russia.

A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia.

Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.

He and his family fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum, as Syria's new authorities began pursuing former officials over alleged crimes committed during the country's civil war.

What did the court say about Assad?

Assad was convicted of the crimes of "premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity."

"The contribution of the criminal Bashar Assad to the crimes was that of the person ultimately responsible for decision-making, mobilizing state institutions to commit them," the judge said.

The verdict was handed down by Damascus' Fourth Criminal Court and read out live on Syrian state television.

Assad, born in 1965, became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez Assad.

He continued his family's decadeslong rule, maintaining the dominance of the Alawite minority in Sunni-majority Syria and the country's close alliance with Iran as well as hostility toward Israel and the US.

The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad.

Assad's brother Maher and several other figures from the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia.

They were convicted of premeditated murder and torture resulting in death.

Assad's cousin sentenced in person

In the same case, the court also handed the death penalty to Atef Najib, a senior security official under Assad's rule and a cousin of the former dictator. He was arrested while trying to flee the country in January 2025 and became one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.

Najib, a former Syrian army brigadier general, headed the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa when the uprising against Assad's government began in 2011.

He appeared in court under tight security, standing inside a cage in a prison uniform as the judge read out the sentence.

The court convicted Najib of crimes including murder, the intentional killing of children under 15 and torture resulting in death, describing the acts as crimes against humanity.

Edited by Rob Turner

entries.title: How one German city is preparing for climate extremes
entries.summary: Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from wildfires to storms is here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel are trying new ideas.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from wildfires to storms is here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel are trying new ideas.

In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.

Human-caused climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink its design, and how it works. It has since become a front-runner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.

Is climate adaptation giving up on fighting climate change?

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage. 

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the US to Quezon City in the Philippines, as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," she added.

Redesigning cities for unavoidable impacts

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.

Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.

"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.

The research requires patience.

"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.

Living differently: No more daytime soccer?

Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter cities in Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall, but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.

How to reach people who don't think about the climate?

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.

At Kiel Week in June, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

"People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.

Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change, because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.

Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.

"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.

Climate adaptation not 'optional'

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: India news: Cockroach party backs Jharkhand student leader Devendra Nath Mahto
entries.summary: Abhijeet Dipke said his party stood firmly behind Mahto, who was hospitalized after police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse protesters marching towards the state Assembly on Monday. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: CJP backs Jharkhand student leader Mahto

Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026

Abhijeet Dipke said his party stood firmly behind Mahto, who was hospitalized after police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse protesters marching towards the state Assembly on Monday. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Cockroach Janta Party's Abhijeet Dipke backed Jharkhand student leader Devendra Nath Mahto
  • Mahto, who is on hunger strike, said his health deteriorated after police used batons to disperse protesters
  • Dipke called Monday's police action 'cruel and inhuman'
  • IPL cricketer Abishek Porel arrested on rape charges
  • Tamil Nadu calls to scrap NEET exam
  • NASA invites Indian space agency ISRO to join Moon Base program

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, August 11: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section NASA invites Indian space agency ISRO to join Moon Base program

NASA invites Indian space agency ISRO to join Moon Base program

The United States' National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has invited India's space agency to join its planned Moon Base program, reports said on Tuesday.

Posting on X, the US Embassy in India account called NASA's program "humanity's first outpost on the Moon."

"The base will drive lunar scientific breakthroughs and prepare for crewed missions to Mars," the embassy posted, adding that more information will be coming soon.

According to the reports, the call for collaboration with Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) comes as the two countries seek to deepen cooperation under the Artemis Accords.

The two sides have also agreed to advance talks on sharing open scientific data under the accords, which aim to promote cooperation in the civil exploration and use of space.

India signed the Artemis Accords in 2023.

Skip next section Airbus sending experts to assist probe into Air India flight's losing altitude

Airbus sending experts to assist probe into Air India flight's losing altitude

Airbus is sending a team of experts to New Delhi to assist India's investigation into an Air India flight that lost about 300 feet (100 meters) in altitude during a Phuket-New Delhi flight last week, injuring 12 people.

The Airbus A320, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members, stabilized and landed safely after the sudden altitude loss.

India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the incident as serious.

"A team of specialists is being dispatched to assist with the investigation," an Airbus spokesperson said on Monday. "Airbus is providing technical assistance to the relevant investigating authorities. We are actively supporting the airline and will provide further information as it becomes available."

The probe comes as authorities await confirmatory results of a psychoactive substance test for the flight's captain. Both pilots have been removed from the flying roster pending the investigation.



Eight passengers and four cabin crew members were admitted to hospitals after landing in the Indian capital.

Skip next section ANALYSIS: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand

ANALYSIS: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand

Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into reported irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Perspectives on AI, ethics and digital inclusion from Kenya, India and Mexico

IN DEPTH: Perspectives on AI, ethics and digital inclusion from Kenya, India and Mexico

In June 2026, DW hosted researchers from Kenya, India and Mexico. During their visit, Prof. Levi Obonyo, Prof. Carlos Vidales and Ms. Neeti Vaid interacted with students, faculty, DW news editors and MDEV managers.

Read more on talks with researchers on AI.

Skip next section Tamil Nadu calls to scrap nationwide medical college entrance examination

Tamil Nadu calls to scrap nationwide medical college entrance examination

Tamil Nadu's state legislature on Tuesday passed a resolution urging the central government to scrap the nationwide medical college entrance examination, media reports said.

Health Minister KG Arunraj said the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) exam undermined social justice and disadvantaged rural and poorer students by increasing reliance on costly coaching centers, according to the reports.

The Tamil Nadu government instead proposed admissions for medical colleges based on students' grades in Class 12.

The motion was supported by all parties, with the lone lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) walking out during the proceedings, reports said.

The NEET exam has been in the news in India since the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) launched a protest following the cancellation of the test in May, after authorities found its question paper was leaked. 

The cancellation of the highly competitive NEET exam sparked outrage across the country.

The CJP protests, which started in New Delhi and then spread across the country, forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month.

Skip next section US court dismisses bribery and fraud charges against billionaire Adani

US court dismisses bribery and fraud charges against billionaire Adani

A US judge dismissed bribery and fraud charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani on Monday after the Trump administration moved to drop the case.

Adani, a close ally of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's, was charged in 2024 with participating in a $265 million (€230 million) scheme to bribe Indian officials to secure solar energy contracts.

His associates were also charged with attempting to obstruct the US investigations by destroying evidence. Adani has denied wrongdoing.

Brooklyn federal judge Nicholas Garaufis criticized the US Justice Department's handling of the decision said the decision to dismiss the 2024 charges was unusual and raised concerns because prosecutors and investigators, including FBI and SEC agents involved in the case, were not consulted.

According to media reports Adani's attorney Robert Giuffra, who is also Donald Trump's personal lawyer, told Justice Department officials in April that if charges were dropped, the billionaire would invest $10 billion in the United States.

Garaufis said he believed that Adani's reported pledge to invest in the US did not influence the Justice Department's decision to drop the case.

In May, court documents showed that Gautam Adani agreed to pay civil penalties of $6 million, while his nephew Sagar Adani, another leader at Adani Green Energy, agreed to pay $12 million in a settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The proposed settlement doesn't include an admission of guilt.

Adani welcomed the ruling, saying his faith in "truth, fairness and the rule of law" remained unwavering.

Skip next section Jharkhand student leader Mahto hospitalized after police use force

Jharkhand student leader Mahto hospitalized after police use force

Student protest leader Devendra Nath Mahto was admitted to a hospital in the eastern state of Jharkhand after taking part in a march to the state legislature on Monday while on a nine-day hunger strike.

Police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching toward the state assembly on Monday in state capital Ranchi.

The students are alleging irregularities in government recruitment exams.

Mahto said his health deteriorated after police used batons to disperse protesters outside the Legislative Assembly.

"At present, my treatment continues under the supervision of doctors," he wrote on X.





Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke also alleged that Mahto was injured by police batons and was experiencing chest pain.

"Be it Jantar Mantar or Jharkhand, such police brutality against students is cruel and inhuman," Dipke wrote on X, alluding to the last month's student protests that forced India's education minister to resign.

Meanwhile, the Jharkhand unit of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused the Hemant Soren-led government of using excessive force, alleging hundreds of students were injured, and called a statewide shutdown on Tuesday.

Earlier on Sunday, the sixth round of talks between student protesters and the government failed to reach a breakthrough following which the protesters announced a march to the state Assembly.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

The student protests in Jharkhand are showing no signs of abating as leader Devendra Nath Mahto was admitted to a hospital after participating in a march to the state legislature while on a nine-day hunger strike. On Monday, police used tear gas, batons and water cannon to disperse thousands of youth protesters.

Meanwhile, a US court on Monday dismissed a case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, a close ally of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, after the Trump administration decided to drop fraud and bribery allegations against him.

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

entries.title: Middle East: Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat
entries.summary: President Donald Trump reportedly used an elaborate ruse to leave the NATO summit in Turkey, amid a credible assassination threat. Meanwhile, oil prices rose as hopes for a deal on the Strait of Hormuz fade. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Trump took secret flight out of Turkey — report

Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026

President Donald Trump reportedly used an elaborate ruse to leave the NATO summit in Turkey, amid a credible assassination threat. Meanwhile, oil prices rose as hopes for a deal on the Strait of Hormuz fade. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Trump took secret flight out of Ankara after July's NATO summit, amid threat from Iran, Washington Post reports
  • US-Iran talks on peace and reopening Strait of Hormuz hit impasse
  • Oil prices steady after massive gains as market loses hope for a deal

Keep reading for the latest developments in the war in Iran and wider conflict in the Middle East from Tuesday, August 11:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Container ship reportedly hit by missile in Gulf of Oman

Container ship reportedly hit by missile in Gulf of Oman

A container ship is believed to have been struck by a missile in the Gulf of Oman, according to maritime security sources.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received a report of an incident involving a commercial vessel and military forces, later correcting the vessel type from a tanker to a container ship.

Initial assessments identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged Vela Nova.

British maritime risk management group Vanguard and a separate maritime security source said the ship was believed to have been hit while sailing around 71 nautical miles (132 kilometers) off Pakistan's coast.

Skip next section Three killed in reported Houthi attack on cargo ship

Three killed in reported Houthi attack on cargo ship

Three crew members have been killed in a reported Houthi attack on a commercial vessel near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Yemeni government-linked sources.

Two Yemeni coast guard sources and two military officials said the Iran-aligned group attacked a deck cargo ship on Tuesday.

Yemeni pro-government broadcaster Al Yumhuriya said the vessel was hit by a missile and that the dead were two Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian.

The ship's name and nationality were not immediately given.

Yemeni government sources said authorities were working to confirm the circumstances of the attack.

Skip next section US has 'swept entire Strait of Hormuz' of mines: Trump

US has 'swept entire Strait of Hormuz' of mines: Trump

President Donald Trump said that the US has cleared the Strait of Hormuz of mines, and that the critical trade route was open to commercial traffic. 

Trump told reporters at the White House that the US had 100% control of the waterway.

"A little bit complex because they [Iran] will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mines. You know, we've mine swept the entire Strait," he said.

Trump's comments came as Washington and Tehran have been negotiating the full reopening of the strait for some time. Iran has linked the route's reopening to concessions from the US and its allies while affirming plans to charge commercial vessels passing through the strait.

Trump responded to the concessions demand saying he too would demand compensation from Iran, for all the people injured or killed in the conflict.

Over the last weekend, US Vice President JD Vance said that Iran had laid a large number of mines in the Strait at he beginning of the war.  

Skip next section READ: Is Iran's middle class being pushed into poverty?

READ: Is Iran's middle class being pushed into poverty?

The war has intensified Iran's economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses.

Read DW's report on growing fears that millions of middle-income families in Iran are slipping closer to poverty.

Skip next section Oil prices steady after increase, as hopes for a deal fade

Oil prices steady after increase, as hopes for a deal fade

Global crude oil prices steadied on Tuesday, after a significant rise amid persisting uncertainty over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. 

Brent crude and US crude futures were both up slightly on Tuesday morning, reaching the highest levels since July 31, after the contracts spiked roughly 5% on Monday.

The price of Brent hovered just under $88 (€76) a barrel, having swing between $72 and $102 last month.

Oil prices have risen around 10% over the past week, fanning inflationary fears and revitalizing expectations of a possible US interest rate hike in 2026.

"We're now in a bit of a Mexican standoff, if you'd like, in terms of who blinks first," Tony Sycamore, ​a market Analyst at IG told Reuters.

"This is going to be almost a war of attrition now," he said. "You probably can see the (oil) market sitting around the $75 to $95 range while we wait ​to see who blinks first."

Skip next section Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report

Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report

US President Donald Trump reportedly departed from Turkey on a secret military flight in July, instead of the flying aboard an older Air Force One plane as announced by the White House.

This was in response to a credible Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported, as the monthslong war continued.

Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit in July. However, he unexpectedly announced he would used an older Air Force One when departing the country, "for old times's sake." The move had then raised question over the donated jet's safety.

Trump boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras but was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Washington Post said, citing corroborating material and a US official familiar with the operation.

Journalists aboard the decoy Air Force One, where they believed to be accompanied by the US President, said they had been advised to keep their window shades closed in the press cabin.

When they inquired about it later, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight."

"But if I go, you go. Right?" he added.

The White House did not directly address the report.

Communications director Steven Cheung told the Post there were "many enemies of America" targeting Trump and that every available tool was being used tocounter threats.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the war in Iran and developments from across the Middle East.

US President Donald Trump reportedly took a secret flight out of Turkey after the NATO summit in July, according to the Washington Post. The report describes how the US President was smuggled into a smaller plane, provoking mental visuals straight out of a Hollywood movie, to thwart a possible assassination attempt by Iran.

Trump meanwhile, has scoffed at Iran's demands of concessions and reparations, saying he too would seek conflict compensations as part of a peace deal. With this, negotiations over a truce and the possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz seem to have hit a wall once more. 

The news had an effect on global markets as well, initially sending oil prices soaring, but they have now stabilized.

Stay tuned!

entries.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
entries.summary: In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
entries.summary: Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants

August 11, 2026

Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

What does Turkey's new PKK law provide?

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

When will the law take effect?

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

What happens to Abdullah Ocalan?

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

What does the PKK say?

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Why is the bill controversial?

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

Why does the conflict matter?

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus.

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah
